core_hypothesis: If long-running serving traces drop previously useful cached state, retrieval quality degrades unless eviction is treated as a first-class control signal.
why_now: Supporting notes report retrieval degradation after eviction under long serving traces.
supporting_observations: Retrieval quality drops after forced cache eviction on long traces.
Existing cards assume cache residency without measuring eviction effects.

nearest_priors.exact_overlap: Studies cache reuse for long-context serving.
nearest_priors.residual_difference: Does not treat eviction as a controllable failure mechanism with a decisive recall comparison.

proposed_mechanism: Eviction-aware retrieval control that conditions lookup on residency state.
source_of_gain: Separates eviction-induced failure from routing error under a forced-eviction comparison.

cheapest_decisive_test.setup: Compare recall before vs after forced cache eviction on the same long-trace workload.
cheapest_decisive_test.expected_runtime_or_cost: single ablated replay on a fixed trace suite; minutes to hours

strongest_baseline: Unmodified cache-reuse serving stack without eviction control
kill_condition: Forced eviction does not change recall relative to the no-eviction control under the same routing policy.
main_uncertainty: Observed degradation may still be explained by routing error rather than eviction.
expected_reviewer_2_objection: This is A+B: ordinary cache reuse plus a trivial eviction flag.
response_to_objection: The claim is not 'add a flag'; it is that eviction is the causal failure mode and must be discriminated by a decisive recall comparison.
evidence_that_would_make_reviewer_correc: If forced eviction leaves recall unchanged while routing ablations explain the drop, the eviction hypothesis is wrong.
notes: Fully synthetic sample for schema illustration. Not from a live pilot corpus. Cheap decisive experiments have not been run. Not a scientific claim.
